cards.front: Short note: Pharmacokinetic changes in pregnancy

points: Reduced gastrointestinal motility delays absorption of oral drugs
Plasma and extracellular fluid volume expand: volume of distribution may rise
Albumin falls but alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises: free fraction of acidic drugs increases, of basic drugs decreases
Marked rise in renal blood flow: polar drugs cleared faster
Hepatic microsomal enzymes induced: many drugs metabolised faster
Changes are greatest in the third trimester
Overall effect is complex and hard to predict

cards.front: Which drug properties govern transfer across the placenta?
cards.back: Lipid solubility (thiopental crosses almost at once and can sedate the newborn), degree of ionisation (succinylcholine and tubocurarine cross slowly), molecular weight (250-500 cross readily, 500-1000 with difficulty, above 1000 very poorly), placental transporters such as P-glycoprotein, and protein binding. Basic drugs with pKa above 7.4 are ion-trapped in the slightly more acidic fetal blood (pH 7.3).

cards.front: What is ion trapping across the placenta, and which drugs does it affect?
cards.back: Fetal blood is slightly more acidic than maternal blood (about pH 7.3 versus 7.4). Basic drugs with a pKa above 7.4 therefore tend to accumulate in the fetus, so fetal exposure can exceed what maternal levels suggest.

cards.front: Salicylate is almost fully ionised, so why does it still cross the placenta readily?
cards.back: The small unionised fraction is highly lipid-soluble and crosses freely. Ionisation alone does not stop transfer. Contrast succinylcholine and tubocurarine, which are highly ionised and cross slowly.

cards.front: Why is heparin preferred to warfarin for anticoagulation in pregnancy?
cards.back: Heparin (including low-molecular-weight heparins) is a large polar molecule that does not cross the placenta, whereas warfarin crosses and is teratogenic; warfarin should be avoided in the first trimester and beyond, because the fetal brain keeps developing.

cards.front: How do placental transporters limit fetal drug exposure? Give examples.
cards.back: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pumps drugs such as vinblastine, doxorubicin and HIV protease inhibitors back into the maternal blood (for protease inhibitors this may raise the risk of vertical HIV transmission). Glyburide is effluxed by BCRP and MRP3 and is also more than 98.8% protein bound, so fetal levels stay lower than maternal.

cards.front: Why can prednisolone be used in a pregnant woman with little fetal corticosteroid exposure?
cards.back: The placenta converts prednisolone to the inactive prednisone, so the fetus is largely spared active steroid. The placenta also oxidises some drugs (e.g. pentobarbital), but may create toxic metabolites (e.g. from ethanol, benzpyrenes).

cards.front: Do large protein drugs such as monoclonal antibodies reach the fetus?
cards.back: Yes. From the second trimester the placenta develops transporters that carry immunoglobulins to the fetus. Biological drugs such as anti-TNF agents have been found in cord blood, with reports of neonatal neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia and disseminated BCG infection.

cards.front: Essay: Drug transfer across the placenta and fetal exposure

points: Placenta is not an absolute barrier: most drugs cross, and polar compounds cross in measurable amounts when the maternal-fetal gradient is high
Maternal physiology also shifts kinetics (larger fluid volume, lower albumin, faster renal and hepatic clearance)
Lipid solubility: thiopental crosses almost at once
Ionisation: succinylcholine and tubocurarine cross slowly; salicylate still crosses via its unionised fraction
Molecular weight: 250-500 cross readily, 500-1000 with difficulty, above 1000 very poorly (heparin)
Very lipid-soluble drugs: transfer limited by placental blood flow
Maternal binding higher than fetal for sulfonamides, barbiturates, phenytoin, local anaesthetics
Fetal pH 7.3 vs maternal 7.4: basic drugs trapped in the fetus
P-glycoprotein pumps vinblastine, doxorubicin and HIV protease inhibitors back to the mother
Glyburide effluxed by BCRP and MRP3, plus very high protein binding
Placenta converts prednisolone to inactive prednisone; may make toxic metabolites from ethanol
Immunoglobulin transporters from the second trimester carry antibodies and anti-TNF drugs
Heparin chosen over warfarin
Prednisolone spares the fetus
Antiretrovirals and maternal drugs for fetal arrhythmia can be given to treat the fetus

cards.front: What are the three stages at which drugs can affect the foetus?
cards.back: Fertilisation and implantation (conception to day 17): pregnancy fails, often unnoticed. Organogenesis (days 18-55): most vulnerable, structural deformities. Growth and development (day 56 onwards): functional and developmental defects, e.g. organ hypoplasia with ACE inhibitors, ductus closure with NSAIDs, masculinisation by androgens and progestins, foetal goitre with antithyroid drugs and lithium.

cards.front: Match: human teratogens and their defects
cards.text: Thalidomide: {{phocomelia}}; warfarin: {{depressed nose}}, eye and hand defects; phenytoin: hypoplastic phalanges, {{cleft lip/palate}}; valproate and carbamazepine: {{neural tube defects}}; stilboestrol: {{vaginal carcinoma}} in teenage daughters; tetracyclines: {{discoloured teeth}}; ACE inhibitors: {{organ hypoplasia}}; lithium: {{heart}} and other defects; isotretinoin: craniofacial, heart and CNS defects; alcohol: {{foetal alcohol syndrome}}; indomethacin/aspirin: premature closure of {{ductus arteriosus}}.

cards.front: What three criteria define a drug as a teratogen?
cards.back: It produces a characteristic set of malformations (selectivity for target organs); it acts at a particular stage of development, such as the organogenesis window of those organs; and its incidence is dose-dependent. Teratogenic effects also include growth restriction, miscarriage, stillbirth and neurocognitive delay.

cards.front: Which supplement reduces neural tube defects, and by how much?
cards.back: Folic acid taken before and during early pregnancy; Katzung cites a reduction in neural tube defects of up to 75%.

cards.front: How has the US FDA changed pregnancy labelling, and why?
cards.back: The old A, B, C, D, X letter categories were removed under rules effective 30 June 2015. Labels now carry narrative sections (Risk Summary, Clinical Considerations, Data) including pregnancy-registry data, and cover lactation and people of reproductive potential. The letters were dropped because about three-quarters of drugs fell into category C, and the grading had become outdated.

cards.front: What points should be covered when counselling a pregnant woman about drug exposure?
cards.back: Fewer than 30 drugs are proven human teratogens and hundreds are known to be safe. The baseline risk of a neonatal abnormality without any exposure is about 3%. The risk of leaving the maternal condition untreated must be weighed (stopping SSRIs for depression has caused serious maternal morbidity). Good counselling has been shown to prevent unnecessary abortions.

cards.front: Why does the stage of exposure change the kind of fetal harm? Give drug examples.
cards.back: Before day 17 the outcome is all-or-none (failure of pregnancy). In organogenesis (days 18-55) structural defects arise, e.g. thalidomide limb defects (phocomelia). From day 56 the effects are functional or growth-related: ACE inhibitors cause hypoplasia of lungs and kidneys, NSAIDs in late pregnancy close the ductus arteriosus, androgens and progestins masculinise a female fetus, and antithyroid drugs or lithium cause fetal goitre.

cards.front: Short note: Teratogenicity

points: Type of malformation depends on the drug and on the stage of exposure
Foetal exposure depends on maternal blood level and duration of drug in maternal circulation
Table of human teratogens lists defects such as limb, cardiac and neural tube defects, growth retardation, and foetal alcohol syndrome
Teratogenic potential must be judged against the background risk of congenital abnormality

cards.front: Why is it wise to avoid all drugs in pregnancy even when a drug has a reassuring FDA category, and what can lower neural tube defects?
cards.back: The FDA graded birth-defect risk in five categories (A safe to X contraindicated), but the grading is outdated for many drugs as evidence accumulates. Only a few exposed mothers deliver a deformed baby, so the exact risk is hard to estimate; hence avoid drugs unless compelling. Folate therapy in pregnancy can reduce neural tube defects, spontaneous or drug-induced.

cards.front: How do mutagenicity and carcinogenicity of a drug arise, and which drugs are implicated?
cards.back: Oxidation of the drug forms reactive intermediates that bind DNA covalently and cause mutations, which can be heritable. If the altered DNA affects proto-oncogenes or their inhibitors, a tumour can follow, usually after 10-40 years. Implicated: anticancer drugs, radioisotopes, estrogens, tobacco. Such drugs are generally not approved, or are withdrawn, unless needed in life-threatening disease.

cards.front: When is infant exposure through breast milk considered negligible, and why avoid stopping breastfeeding needlessly?
cards.back: When the infant receives under 10% of the weight-corrected maternal dose, toxicity is unlikely. Most drugs reach milk only in small amounts, while formula feeding carries higher infant illness and death, so stopping is not free of harm.

cards.front: How can a mother time a relatively safe drug to minimise infant exposure?
cards.back: Take it 30-60 minutes after nursing and 3-4 hours before the next feed, so milk levels are lowest when the baby feeds. A drug such as chloral hydrate can sedate the infant if feeding falls at the peak milk concentration.

cards.front: Which drugs reach clinically meaningful levels in breast milk?
cards.back: Lithium, amiodarone and atenolol. Lithium reaches a milk concentration equal to the mother's serum level, so infant exposure can be large.

cards.front: Why is codeine risky for breastfeeding mothers?
cards.back: Mothers who are CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers make much more morphine, which passes into milk; a neonatal death from opioid toxicity was traced to this. Neonates are also extra sensitive because their blood-brain barrier has little P-glycoprotein, so more morphine enters the brain. The FDA issued a warning on codeine-containing painkillers in lactation.

cards.front: Why are tetracycline, isoniazid, chloramphenicol and radioiodine a concern during breastfeeding?
cards.back: Tetracycline stains the infant's developing teeth permanently. Isoniazid can cause infant pyridoxine deficiency, so the mother should take pyridoxine. Chloramphenicol risks marrow suppression, so it is advised against. Radioiodine suppresses the infant's thyroid and may raise later thyroid cancer risk up to 10-fold; breastfeeding is stopped after large doses and withheld after small ones.

cards.front: How should sedatives and opioids be handled in a breastfeeding mother?
cards.back: Hypnotic barbiturates cause infant lethargy and poor suck; diazepam sedates and accumulates because of its long half-life. Chronic maternal opioid use can prolong neonatal dependence. Methadone may be continued under supervision without abrupt stopping, with the infant watched for withdrawal; codeine is risky if the mother is a CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser.

cards.front: Short note: Drug use during lactation

points: Most drugs appear in milk, usually in low amounts
Infant dose below 10% of the maternal weight-corrected dose: toxicity unlikely
Formula feeding carries higher infant morbidity, so avoid needless stopping of breastfeeding
Take a relatively safe drug 30-60 min after a feed and 3-4 h before the next
Lithium: milk level equals maternal serum
Amiodarone, atenolol: clinically meaningful exposure
Tetracycline: milk about 70% of serum, tooth staining
Isoniazid: pyridoxine deficiency unless mother supplemented
Barbiturates, chloral hydrate, diazepam: sedation; diazepam accumulates
Methadone: breastfeeding possible with care; taper slowly
Codeine in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser mothers: neonatal opioid death; FDA warning

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacokinetics in the neonate

points: Low gastric acid (slower rise in preterm) and gastric emptying up to 6-8 h
Irregular peristalsis; low bile acids and lipase
Thin skin: faster transdermal absorption; rectal absorption fast and reliable
Erratic i.m. absorption in sick preterm infants with poor perfusion
Body water 70-75% (preterm 85%) vs adult 50-60%; extracellular water 40% vs 20%
Larger volume for water-soluble drugs (aminoglycosides)
Lower protein binding: more free drug
Leaky blood-brain barrier
CYP and conjugation activity 50-70% of adult
Glucuronidation matures by 3-4 years
Chloramphenicol gray baby syndrome
GFR 30-40% of adult at birth; reaches adult values by 6-12 months (Katzung)
Half-life of gentamicin and penicillin prolonged 3-5 times (KDT)

cards.front: How should a child's dose be calculated, and why not with old age-based formulae?
cards.back: Preferably by body weight (mg/kg), as most manufacturers recommend. Age-based formulae are no longer used. Infant doses must be learnt as such, because infants differ physiologically from adults and cannot be dosed from a formula.

cards.front: Name four adverse effects that occur particularly in growing children.
cards.back: Growth suppression with corticosteroids; early epiphyseal fusion and stunting with androgens; tetracycline deposition in growing teeth causing discolouration and deformity; dystonic reactions to phenothiazines are more frequent.

cards.front: Why can metered-dose inhalers and solid dosage forms be a problem in young children?
cards.back: Young children find solid dosage forms and metered-dose inhalers difficult to administer.

cards.front: How can drugs cause kernicterus in a neonate, and which drug is avoided for this reason?
cards.back: Some drugs displace bilirubin from albumin; because the neonatal blood-brain barrier is permeable, free bilirubin enters the brain. This happened when sulfonamides were given to preterm neonates. Ceftriaxone is avoided completely in infants under 2 months. Conversely, rising bilirubin can displace drugs such as phenytoin and raise their free level.

cards.front: Why do toddlers and young children often need a higher mg/kg dose than adults?
cards.back: After the first year, drug metabolism and renal elimination often exceed adult rates. The half-lives of theophylline, phenytoin and carbamazepine are shorter than in adults, and the daily per-kg digoxin dose is higher in children (KDT: about 8-12 microgram/kg vs 3-5 microgram/kg in adults).

cards.front: What practical problems with dosage forms and adherence occur in paediatric practice?
cards.back: Suspensions (e.g. phenytoin) must be shaken each time or early doses are weak and late doses toxic; elixirs need no shaking. Household teaspoons vary from 2.5 to 7.8 mL, so a calibrated spoon or syringe should be used. Parents often stop antibiotics once the child feels well. Weight-based calculations risk tenfold decimal errors (e.g. digoxin): use a leading zero, avoid trailing zeros and double-check high-risk drugs.

cards.front: Why is the digoxin dose per kg higher in children, yet it accumulates in neonates?
cards.back: Toddlers clear digoxin faster than adults, so the dose per kg is much higher. Neonates eliminate it slowly (digoxin half-life 60-70 h in neonates vs 30-60 h in adults) because renal clearance is immature, so it accumulates.

cards.front: Short note: Drug therapy in neonates

points: Infants are not small adults
Renal clearance is low and tubular transport immature at birth
Conjugation is inefficient, so drugs such as chloramphenicol accumulate
Grey baby syndrome occurs after high doses, especially in premature neonates
Feeding stops, vomiting and hypotonia follow
Benzyl alcohol preservative has been linked to a fatal toxic syndrome in neonates
Unpreserved epoetin is therefore used for anaemia of prematurity

cards.front: Short note: Principles of drug administration in children

points: Children's dose can be calculated on body weight: child weight (kg) / 70 x average adult dose
Body surface area is argued to be a more accurate basis for dose calculation
Oral drops are the preferred dosage form for infants and young children

Rectal route (suppository or retention enema) can be used with recurrent vomiting or unconsciousness; in general absorption is slower and less predictable, though diazepam solution and paracetamol suppository are dependably absorbed. In infants and young children rectal absorption is fast and predictable, which is why diazepam solution is given rectally for febrile seizures under 5 years
Children can react more strongly: a single triflupromazine dose causes muscular dystonias in some, especially children

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacokinetic changes in the elderly

points: Little real change; slower gastric emptying and reduced gut motility and blood flow may slow it
Less lean mass and body water, more fat
Volume of distribution rises for lipophilic and falls for hydrophilic drugs
Albumin falls; alpha-1 acid glycoprotein may rise
Hepatic blood flow falls to about 55-60% of young adult
Phase I (CYP) affected more than phase II conjugation
Lower clearance of e.g. diazepam, imipramine, propranolol, theophylline; not of lorazepam, oxazepam, warfarin
GFR about 75% at 50 years and 50% at 75 years (KDT)
Serum creatinine misleads because muscle mass falls; estimate creatinine clearance from age, weight and serum creatinine

cards.front: Write the formula used to estimate creatinine clearance in an elderly patient.
cards.back: CLcr (mL/min) = (140 - age) x weight (kg) / (72 x serum creatinine in mg/dL); multiply by 0.85 for women. It is only a population estimate; up to a third of elderly people have normal renal function, and a timed 12- or 24-h clearance is needed for precision.

cards.front: What is the Beers criteria?
cards.back: A list of potentially inappropriate medications for older persons. It is organised by body system and therapeutic category, and gives the rationale and quality of evidence for each entry.

cards.front: What do the START and STOPP tools do in prescribing for older patients?
cards.back: START lists evidence-based prescribing indicators by body system, to alert the prescriber to the right treatment. STOPP identifies potentially inappropriate medicines in older persons' prescriptions and is used for medication review.

cards.front: What does the Medication Appropriateness Index check for each prescribed drug?
cards.back: Whether the drug is indicated, whether it is effective, whether the dose is appropriate, whether it is cost-effective, and whether it duplicates another therapy.

cards.front: Give examples of altered drug sensitivity in the elderly.
cards.back: More sensitive to sedative-hypnotics and to respiratory depression by opioids; relatively intolerant to digitalis; reduced responsiveness to beta-adrenoceptor agonists and antagonists; even mild anticholinergic action worsens voiding in men with prostatism; phenothiazines cause more orthostatic hypotension. Benzodiazepine and barbiturate half-lives rise by 50-150% between 30 and 70 years.

cards.front: Why are adverse drug reactions so common in the elderly, and what is a 'brown bag' review?
cards.back: ADR incidence is at least twice that of younger people, rising from about 10% with one drug to nearly 100% with ten. Causes: altered kinetics, several prescribers, OTC and herbal products, interactions (e.g. cimetidine inhibiting metabolism of phenytoin, warfarin, beta blockers) and nonadherence. In a brown bag review the patient brings every medicine and supplement; duplicates and unnecessary drugs are removed, often cutting the total by 30-50%.

cards.front: State the principles of prescribing for geriatric patients.
cards.back: Take a careful drug history; prescribe only for a specific rational indication; define the goal, start low and titrate, waiting at least three (age-adjusted) half-lives before increasing; check blood levels if the usual dose fails; keep a high suspicion for reactions and interactions, including OTC and herbal products; simplify the regimen and reduce the number of drugs.

cards.front: How should digoxin loading and maintenance doses be adjusted in an elderly patient?
cards.back: Reduce the loading dose because the apparent volume of distribution is smaller (less lean mass and water), and reduce the maintenance dose because renal clearance is lower.

cards.front: Essay: Drug therapy in special populations

points: Kinetic changes: larger Vd, altered binding, faster renal and hepatic clearance
Placental transfer: lipid solubility, ionisation, size, transporters
Teratogenic stages; known teratogens; FDA narrative labelling since 2015
Avoid drugs unless compelling; folate supplementation
Most drugs low in milk; under 10% infant dose is safe
Concern: lithium, amiodarone, atenolol, tetracycline, sedatives, codeine
Immature metabolism and GFR; more body water; leaky BBB
Gray baby, kernicterus
Faster clearance in toddlers; weight-based dosing; dosage-form errors
Reduced renal clearance; estimated creatinine clearance
Altered Vd and phase I metabolism; more sensitivity to CNS drugs
Polypharmacy, ADRs, brown bag review; start low, go slow
Higher bioavailability, low albumin, reduced clearance
Prefer oxazepam/lorazepam; avoid hepatotoxins
Reduce maintenance dose by CLcr; loading dose unchanged
Avoid nephrotoxins, pethidine, K-sparing diuretics, thiazides

cards.front: What parameters make up the Child-Pugh score, and what are the classes?
cards.back: The score uses bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy. Class A (mild) is 5-6 points, class B (moderate) 7-9 points and class C (severe) 10-15 points. Class B and C patients have decompensated cirrhosis.

cards.front: Why is ponesimod not recommended in some patients with liver disease?
cards.back: It is not recommended for patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment, that is Child-Pugh class B or C.

cards.front: Which fluoroquinolone is avoided in liver disease, and which was withdrawn for hepatotoxicity?
cards.back: Pefloxacin is listed among antimicrobials to avoid in liver disease, and it is mainly eliminated by the liver. Trovafloxacin was hepatotoxic and was withdrawn from the US market.

cards.front: Short note: Child-Pugh score

points: Encephalopathy: none / grade 1-2 / grade 3-4
Ascites: none / slight / moderate
Bilirubin: below 2 / 2 to 3 / above 3
Albumin: above 3.5 / 2.8 to 3.5 / below 2.8
Prothrombin time: under 4 s / 4 to 6 s / over 6 s (INR often used: below 1.7 / 1.7 to 2.2 / above 2.2)
Class A: 5 to 6 points
Class B: 7 to 9 points
Class C: 10 to 15 points
Estimates mortality in cirrhosis
Elective surgery contraindicated in class C

refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Use of the Child Pugh Score in Liver Disease (2023) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542308/

cards.front: One cited study: one-year mortality by Child-Pugh class?
cards.back: Class A 0%, class B 20%, class C 55%.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Use of the Child Pugh Score in Liver Disease (2023) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542308/

cards.front: How does cirrhosis change drug handling, per the expert panel's introduction?
cards.back: Reduced metabolic capacity, decreased protein synthesis and portosystemic shunting.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: Which Child-Pugh stages did the cirrhosis dosing panel cover?
cards.back: Stages A, B and C.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: What three recommendation options did the panel use for each drug?
cards.back: No dose adjustment, dose adjustment, or avoidance of administration.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: How is the starting dose of obeticholic acid set according to liver disease stage?
cards.back: Used when there is no adequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid after at least 1 year, or when it is not tolerated. Non-cirrhotic or Child-Pugh A: start 5 mg once daily for 3 months, then 10 mg once daily at most. Child-Pugh B or C, or a prior decompensation event: start 5 mg once weekly for 3 months, then 5 mg twice weekly, at most 10 mg twice weekly (doses at least 3 days apart).

cards.front: Why is succinylcholine unsafe in hepatic failure?
cards.back: Succinylcholine is broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase. An acquired deficiency of this enzyme, as in liver disease, predisposes to prolonged apnoea, so the drug is unsafe there.

cards.front: Which antitubercular drugs are safe in liver disease, and which is most hepatotoxic?
cards.back: Streptomycin and ethambutol are non-hepatotoxic and are used when the liver is damaged, with a fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin. Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic, followed by rifampicin; isoniazid is also hepatotoxic. On rechallenge after hepatitis, drugs are restarted one at a time in the order rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide.
refs: Case-Based Learning in Pharmacology PDF p225

cards.front: Does a Child-Pugh class alone decide the dose of a drug?
cards.back: No. Dosing decisions rely on the drug's prescribing information, not the score alone. Reassess the score when the patient's condition changes.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Use of the Child Pugh Score in Liver Disease (2023) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542308/

cards.front: How did expert agreement change with Child-Pugh severity?
cards.back: It fell: about 83% agreement in stage A, 47% in B and 41% in C.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: What did the panel's consensus recommendations mostly say?
cards.back: No dose adjustment or avoidance.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: Why is cirrhosis dosing hard to apply, per the panel?
cards.back: Stage-specific dosing guidance is inconsistent and prescribing information is often unclear.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: Did pharmacists and hepatologists favour the same advice?
cards.back: No. Pharmacists and clinical pharmacologists more often advised dose adjustment; hepatologists more often chose standard dosing or avoidance.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

cards.front: Why do high-extraction drugs given orally need a large dose cut in cirrhosis?
cards.back: Their clearance depends on liver blood flow and first-pass extraction. In cirrhosis, portosystemic shunting and loss of hepatocytes let much more of an oral dose escape first-pass metabolism, so bioavailability and blood levels rise sharply (e.g. morphine, propranolol).

cards.front: In hepatic impairment, how are loading and maintenance doses handled?
cards.back: Loading dose depends on volume of distribution and is usually unchanged (it may even need to be larger if ascites expands the volume of a water-soluble drug). Maintenance dose depends on clearance, so it is reduced or the interval lengthened as Child-Pugh class worsens.

cards.front: What drug problems arise in liver disease apart from reduced clearance?
cards.back: Cirrhosis markedly increases CNS sensitivity to morphine and barbiturates (coma at normal doses). Brisk diuresis in impending encephalopathy causes hypokalaemic alkalosis, converting NH4+ to NH3 that enters the brain. Oral anticoagulants prolong prothrombin time sharply because clotting factors are already low. Prodrugs needing hepatic activation work less well.

cards.front: Short note: Drug therapy in liver disease

points: Bioavailability of high first-pass drugs rises (loss of hepatocytes, portocaval shunting)
Low albumin: more free acidic drugs (diclofenac, warfarin)
Reduced clearance of morphine, lidocaine, propranolol: lower doses
Prodrugs needing hepatic activation (bacampicillin) less effective
Oxazepam or lorazepam instead of diazepam
Atenolol as the beta blocker
Morphine and barbiturates may cause coma in cirrhotics
Brisk diuresis: hypokalaemic alkalosis, more NH3, hepatic encephalopathy
Oral anticoagulants markedly prolong prothrombin time
NSAID fluid retention and metformin lactic acidosis worsen
No simple test (unlike creatinine clearance) predicts the change
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs

cards.front: Short note: Dose adjustment in hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh approach)

points: A: mild, compensated; most drugs at usual dose, care with narrow-margin drugs
B: moderate; reduce dose or lengthen interval of hepatically cleared drugs and monitor
C: severe; avoid drugs cleared mainly by the liver and hepatotoxic drugs unless the label allows a reduced dose
Oral bioavailability rises with shunting and lost hepatocytes (morphine, propranolol, lidocaine)
Reduce the oral dose markedly
Clearance falls with enzyme capacity; free fraction rises when albumin is low
Reduce the maintenance dose or lengthen the interval; loading dose usually unchanged
Prefer drugs cleared by the kidney or by glucuronidation (lorazepam, oxazepam)
Avoid sedatives, NSAIDs and drugs that precipitate encephalopathy or bleeding
Start low, titrate slowly, monitor effect and levels
No test of liver function predicts drug clearance the way creatinine clearance does for the kidney
Label advice comes from studies grouped by Child-Pugh class; follow it

cards.front: Classify: antimicrobials needing dose reduction in renal failure
cards.text: Even in mild failure: {{aminoglycosides}}, {{cephalexin}}, {{ethambutol}}, {{vancomycin}}, {{amphotericin B}}, {{acyclovir}}. Only in severe failure: {{cotrimoxazole}}, {{carbenicillin}}, {{cefotaxime}}, {{norfloxacin}}, {{ciprofloxacin}}, {{metronidazole}}.

cards.front: In renal impairment, how should the dose change relate to clearance?
cards.back: Reduce the dose in proportion to the calculated fall in drug clearance.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

cards.front: Which CKD stage requires renal replacement therapy, and what GFR defines it?
cards.back: Stage 5, with a GFR of 14 to 0 mL/min.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

cards.front: Which creatinine equation has largely replaced older methods for estimating kidney function?
cards.back: The CKD-EPI creatinine equation, recommended by the NKF and ASN task force; older methods were Cockcroft-Gault and MDRD.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

cards.front: Why does protein binding limit how much drug dialysis removes?
cards.back: Only unbound drug crosses the dialysis membrane, so the bound fraction is not available for removal.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

cards.front: Which drugs are mainly removed by diffusion during dialysis?
cards.back: Small molecules; drugs under about 1000 daltons are mainly removed this way.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

cards.front: How are doses of renally excreted drugs adjusted in kidney disease?
cards.back: Clearance of drugs excreted unchanged (aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone) falls in parallel with creatinine clearance. Loading dose is unchanged (unless oedema), but maintenance dose is cut or interval lengthened. KDT guide: CLcr 50-70 mL/min, 70% of the dose rate; 30-50, 50%; 10-30, 30%; 5-10, 20%. Steady state is reached later if half-life is prolonged.

cards.front: Which drugs should be avoided or used with care in renal failure, and why?
cards.back: Nephrotoxic drugs: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines (except doxycycline; also anti-anabolic, worsen uraemia), sulfonamides (crystalluria), vancomycin, nitrofurantoin, cyclosporine, amphotericin B. Thiazides are ineffective and reduce GFR (use furosemide). Potassium-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalaemia. Pethidine: norpethidine accumulates and causes seizures. Urinary antiseptics fail to reach urinary levels and cause systemic toxicity. NSAIDs increase fluid retention.

cards.front: How does renal failure alter drug distribution and sensitivity?
cards.back: Albumin is low or altered, so binding of acidic drugs falls (basic drugs little changed). The blood-brain barrier becomes more permeable, so opiates, barbiturates, phenothiazines and benzodiazepines cause more CNS depression. Antihypertensives cause more postural hypotension.

cards.front: How does haemodialysis change the vancomycin dosing schedule?
cards.back: With non-high-flux dialysis membranes, about 1 g (around 15 mg/kg) every 5 to 7 days typically gives adequate levels. With intermittent high-efficiency or high-flux dialysis, maintenance doses are needed after each dialysis session.

cards.front: Why are renal dose changes usually coarse, and when is more care needed?
cards.back: Changes are often halving or doubling, since a 20% change is usually impractical. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index need more careful adjustment.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

cards.front: Why must dialysis dosing be reviewed as residual kidney function changes?
cards.back: Residual renal function clears renally excreted drugs, and it can change daily, so dosing should be reassessed as it improves or declines.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

cards.front: For intermittent drugs in dialysis, what timing point matters?
cards.back: Exposure depends on the dose timing relative to the start and length of the session, so these doses are planned around dialysis.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

cards.front: Why are pethidine, thiazides and potassium-sparing diuretics problematic in renal failure?
cards.back: Pethidine: norpethidine accumulates on repeated dosing and causes seizures and twitching. Thiazides are ineffective and can worsen uraemia, so furosemide is used. Potassium-sparing diuretics are contraindicated because of hyperkalaemia and cardiac depression.

cards.front: In extended dialysis (SLED), what do studies suggest to replace drug removed during a session?
cards.back: Giving a dose after the session, or both before and after it.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

cards.front: Can intermittent haemodialysis dosing advice be applied straight to SLED?
cards.back: Not safely: it may underdose and risk treatment failure, and the evidence base for SLED is small.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

cards.front: Essay: Prescribing drugs in renal impairment

points: Estimate function with creatinine clearance; the fall in clearance with age is not mirrored by serum creatinine because muscle mass and creatinine production also fall
Clearance of unchanged drugs falls in parallel with creatinine clearance
Albumin low or altered: acidic drug binding falls
Blood-brain barrier more permeable: more CNS depression with opiates, barbiturates, phenothiazines, benzodiazepines
Loading dose unchanged (unless oedema); cut maintenance dose or lengthen interval
Dose rate as % of normal by creatinine clearance: 50-70 mL/min 70%, 30-50 50%, 10-30 30%, 5-10 20%
Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, acyclovir need reduction even in mild failure
Tetracyclines (except doxycycline), sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, cyclosporine are nephrotoxic or worsen uraemia
Thiazides ineffective; potassium-sparing diuretics contraindicated; pethidine accumulates norpethidine

cards.front: Give examples of gastrointestinal disease altering drug absorption.
cards.back: In coeliac disease amoxicillin absorption falls but cephalexin and cotrimoxazole absorption rises, so malabsorption does not reduce all drugs. Gastric stasis in a migraine attack delays absorption. Achlorhydria reduces aspirin absorption by increasing its ionisation.

cards.front: How is the dose calculated for an exceptionally obese or lean adult?
cards.back: On a body weight basis: individual dose = (body weight in kg / 70) x average adult dose. The average adult dose refers to a person of medium build. Body surface area has been argued to be a more accurate basis.

cards.front: Why do myasthenia gravis patients need special care with neuromuscular blockers?
cards.back: Myasthenic patients are very sensitive to curare-type drugs, and quinine aggravates their weakness.

cards.front: How do achlorhydria and peptic ulcer disease alter drug handling?
cards.back: Achlorhydria reduces aspirin absorption by favouring its ionisation. In peptic ulcer disease, NSAIDs can aggravate the ulcer, so avoid them.

cards.front: How does congestive heart failure alter drug kinetics?
cards.back: Absorption falls from mucosal oedema and splanchnic vasoconstriction (procainamide, hydrochlorothiazide); volume of distribution may change, so loading doses of lidocaine and procainamide should be lowered; elimination slows from hepatic congestion and low GFR, so dosing rates of lidocaine, procainamide and theophylline may need cutting; the failing heart is more sensitive to digitalis.

cards.front: How does thyroid status alter drug response?
cards.back: Hypothyroid patients are more sensitive to digoxin, morphine and CNS depressants. Hyperthyroid patients resist the inotropic action of digoxin but are more prone to its arrhythmias. Digoxin clearance roughly follows thyroid function.

cards.front: Compare how heart failure, hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism change the response to digitalis.
cards.back: Failing heart: more sensitive to digitalis. Hypothyroid: more sensitive to digoxin (with morphine and CNS depressants). Hyperthyroid: resists its inotropic action yet is more prone to its arrhythmias. Digoxin clearance roughly follows thyroid function, which explains only part of the change.

cards.front: Short note: Effect of disease states on drug response

points: Absorption falls (mucosal oedema, splanchnic vasoconstriction)
Lower loading doses of lidocaine and procainamide
Slower elimination of lidocaine, procainamide, theophylline; more sensitive to digitalis
Hypothyroid: more sensitive to digoxin, morphine, CNS depressants
Hyperthyroid: resists digoxin inotropy, more arrhythmias
Coeliac: amoxicillin absorption falls, cephalexin and cotrimoxazole rises
Migraine stasis delays absorption; achlorhydria cuts aspirin absorption
NSAIDs aggravate ulcers
Myasthenia: very sensitive to curare-type drugs
See renal and hepatic cards: dose by clearance, check binding and CNS sensitivity
Obese or lean adult: dose = body weight/70 x average dose; surface area argued better

cards.front: What is orthostatic (postural) hypotension, and why does it matter in older patients?
cards.back: A fall in blood pressure on standing. Homeostatic reflexes are blunted with age, and symptomatic orthostatic hypotension becomes much more common, so older patients cannot compensate. Alpha-1 blocking drugs make it worse. The result is dizziness and falls.

cards.front: Which antihypertensive causes postural hypotension, and what injury can follow in an elderly patient?
cards.back: Prazosin (alpha-1 blocker). Postural hypotension, mainly with the first dose or with dose increments, can cause a fall with fracture of the neck of femur in an elderly patient. Starting with a low dose at bedtime minimises it.

cards.front: Why do antipsychotics and tricyclics add to fall risk in the elderly?
cards.back: Alpha-1 blockade causes orthostatic hypotension; low-potency first-generation antipsychotics carry more of this risk than high-potency ones. Tricyclics also block H1 receptors (sedation) and muscarinic receptors (cognitive dulling and confusion).

cards.front: How does polypharmacy in older patients raise the chance of a fall?
cards.back: Elderly patients take several drugs for hypertension, heart disease, diabetes and arthritis. Each added drug multiplies the chance of an interaction, and the combined effects on blood pressure and the CNS cause postural instability, giddiness and confusion. ADRs are much more common in the elderly.

cards.front: Short note: Drugs that increase fall risk in the elderly, with prescribing concerns

points: GFR about 75% of the young-adult value at 50 years and about 50% at 75
Reduced hepatic microsomal activity and liver blood flow
Lower plasma albumin and slower absorption; cumulative toxicity with prolonged use
Benzodiazepine and barbiturate half-lives rise 50-150% between ages 30 and 70; lorazepam and oxazepam less affected
Relatively intolerant to digitalis
Responsiveness of beta-adrenergic receptors to agonists and antagonists is reduced
Mild anticholinergic activity can worsen voiding in elderly males with prostatism
Multiple drugs for hypertension, heart disease, diabetes and arthritis raise interaction risk
ADR incidence is much higher and rises with the number of drugs
Alpha-1 blockers and other antihypertensives: postural hypotension; prazosin can fracture the neck of femur
Antipsychotics: low-potency FGAs and alpha-1 blocking agents cause orthostasis; sedation and EPS add to risk
Tricyclics: alpha-1 orthostasis, H1 sedation and anticholinergic confusion
Any drug causing dizziness adds to postural instability
Start low and titrate slowly; antipsychotic doses in older patients are often about 50% of the younger dose
Postural hypotension is worst with the first dose and with dose increments: start low (prazosin at bedtime) and titrate slowly
Review and cut drugs without a clear indication

cards.front: Why do women usually need doses at the lower end of the range?
cards.back: Women have a smaller body size, so their doses are kept on the lower side of the usual range.

cards.front: Which sex hormones are unacceptable to the opposite sex?
cards.back: Androgens are unacceptable to women and estrogens to men, so sex hormone prescribing must match the patient's sex.

cards.front: Which drugs affect sexual function or breast tissue only in men?
cards.back: Clonidine, methyldopa, beta-blockers and diuretics can impair sexual function in males but not females. Gynaecomastia from ketoconazole, metoclopramide, chlorpromazine or digitalis occurs only in men.

cards.front: How do pregnancy changes alter drug disposition?
cards.back: Reduced GI motility delays absorption; plasma volume expands; albumin falls while alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises, so the free fraction of acidic drugs rises and of basic drugs falls. Renal blood flow rises, speeding elimination of polar drugs, and hepatic enzymes are induced. The net effect is complex. Menstruation and lactation also need review.

cards.front: Why does citalopram exposure differ between women and men?
cards.back: The R-enantiomer of citalopram is cleared more slowly in women than in men, so women have higher exposure to it. This is a reported sex-based pharmacokinetic difference.

cards.front: What do the data show about sex differences in opioid analgesia?
cards.back: Females account for most chronic pain syndromes. Acute-pain studies report either no sex difference or greater sensitivity in females. The duration of morphine analgesia increases progressively with age, though the degree of analgesia at a given dose is similar.

cards.front: Short note: Gender-based differences in drug therapy

points: Smaller body size: doses on the lower side of the range
Subjective effects of drugs may differ in females
Citalopram R-enantiomer cleared more slowly in women, so exposure is higher
Androgens unacceptable to women; estrogens unacceptable to men
Sexual dysfunction from clonidine, methyldopa, beta-blockers and diuretics occurs in men, not women
Gynaecomastia (ketoconazole, metoclopramide, chlorpromazine, digitalis) occurs only in men
Consider menstruation, pregnancy and lactation before prescribing
Pregnancy: reduced GI motility, expanded volume, higher renal blood flow, hepatic enzyme induction
Major depression about twice as frequent in women; some evidence for sex-based response to antidepressants
Maintenance digoxin in heart failure reported with higher mortality in women than men (association)
Females have most chronic pain syndromes
Acute-pain studies: no sex difference or greater sensitivity in females

cards.front: How common is major depression in women compared with men?
cards.back: About twice as frequent. There is some evidence for a sex-based difference in response to antidepressant drugs.

cards.front: Why is maintenance digoxin in heart failure a concern for women?
cards.back: Maintenance digoxin in heart failure has been reported to carry higher mortality in women than in men. The book describes this as an association, not a settled cause, so women on digoxin need careful review.

cards.front: Short note: clearance of drugs at the extremes of age (neonate versus elderly)

sections.h: Clearance and why age changes it
points: Clearance is the theoretical volume of plasma cleared of drug in unit time, and equals rate of elimination divided by plasma concentration; it is the sum of renal, hepatic and other clearances
At both extremes the two clearing organs fall short, so clearance is low and half-life long, but the cause is opposite: immaturity at birth, loss of nephrons and liver mass in old age
Because clearance sets the maintenance dose, both groups need dose or interval changes even when the loading dose is unchanged
At birth glomerular filtration is only 30-40% of adult values when corrected for surface area, and lower still before 34 weeks of gestation

It rises to 50-60% of adult by the end of the third week and reaches adult values between 6 and 12 months; KDT8 puts adult filtration at about 5 months of age and maturation of tubular secretion at about 7 months
The result is a 3-5 fold longer half-life of drugs cleared by filtration (gentamicin) or secretion (penicillin); preterm infants clear penicillins at about 17% of the adult rate
Toddlerhood overshoots the adult: filtration and metabolism per kilogram exceed adult values, so bigger per-kilogram doses are needed (digoxin)
Neonatal CYP450 and conjugating activity reach only 50-70% of adult levels, and glucuronidation matures only between the third and fourth years
Half-lives are correspondingly long: phenobarbital about 200 hours in the first 5 days against 64-140 hours in adults, and phenytoin about 80 hours at 0-2 days against 12-18 hours
Chloramphenicol is the classic casualty of slow glucuronidation (gray baby syndrome)

After the first year, drugs are usually metabolized faster than in adults, so theophylline, phenytoin and carbamazepine have shorter half-lives and need higher per-kilogram doses; drug exposure in utero to an inducer such as phenobarbital can mature the neonatal enzymes early
Glomerular filtration falls to about 75% of the young adult value at 50 years and about 50% at 75 years, with kidney weight at about 80%

Creatinine clearance declines with age in about two thirds of people, but serum creatinine barely rises because muscle mass and creatinine production fall together, so a normal creatinine can hide a low clearance
Estimate creatinine clearance with the Cockcroft-Gault equation and multiply by 0.85 in women; up to a third of healthy elderly have no fall, so the estimate can under-dose an individual patient
Most drugs are cleared by the kidney substantially more slowly after 75 years
Liver blood flow is 55-60% of the young adult value, and microsomal phase I oxidation falls more than phase II conjugation, so clearance of high-extraction drugs falls partly for flow reasons
Clearance is reduced for diazepam, imipramine, propranolol, theophylline, tolbutamide and others, but not for lorazepam, oxazepam or warfarin
Oral bioavailability of high first-pass drugs generally rises, and slower recovery from liver injury, malnutrition and heart failure add to the fall
Low clearance means a longer half-life, a later steady state and accumulation to toxic levels on repeated dosing - the cumulative toxicity of the elderly and of the neonate on long therapy

Maintenance dose is proportional to clearance, so reduce the dose or lengthen the interval; loading dose depends on volume of distribution instead, which is reduced for digoxin in the elderly but expanded for water-soluble drugs in the neonate
Neonatal doses must be taken from age-specific schedules and not derived from adult formulae; where renal function in a sick infant is unpredictable, adjust against measured plasma concentrations
In the elderly, dose to estimated renal function and re-check it as the patient ages, since the same serum creatinine means less clearance at 80 than at 40
